title: Electrode and process design for regulation of liquid metal embrittlement phenomenon during spot welding of dual-phase steel: numerical modelling and experiments
abstract: Abstract Thermal and mechanical loading, combined with zinc coating, are the primary factors influencing liquid metal embrittlement (LME) in the investigated advanced high-strength dual-phase steel, with a yield strength of 1200 MPa and high ductility during resistance spot welding. LME results in a ductility loss of up to 95% and is driven by an intergranular decohesion mechanism, leading to brittle failure in otherwise ductile steel. Validated numerical models provide deeper insights into the critical conditions during welding. The presented multi-physical model enables the optimisation of welding parameters, reducing experimental efforts and enhancing manufacturing efficiency. This study introduces new methods to reduce LME while improving overall weld quality. Surface-coated refractory electrodes significantly reduce embrittlement compared to standard copper electrodes. For copper electrodes, a newly developed shape minimises stresses and misalignment-induced stresses, further reducing embrittlement and enhancing weldability. Additionally, a mandatory holding time after welding effectively lowers embrittlement, while interrupted cooling creates critical conditions. Downward ramped current improves surface conditions, rendering the weld spot less susceptible to embrittlement.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Developments in the automotive industry, such as advancements in e-mobility, enhanced safety features, and stricter emission reduction, lead to an increasing demand for lightweight steels with high strength. Among these materials, dual-phase (DP) steels, which are the focus of this investigation, are widely used in structural components like the B-pillar in automobiles. The key advantage lies in their unique microstructure, which consists of a soft ferrite matrix interspersed with hard martensite islands. Controlled cooling results in a fraction of retained austenite, which further enhances the material’s properties [ 1 ,  2 ].

For advanced high-strength dual-phase steel with a yield strength of 1200 MPa and high ductility (DP1200HD), the preferred joining process is resistance spot welding (RSW). This process is reliable, cost-efficient, and automatable, ensuring the formation of strong, inseparable joints. RSW operates by joining metals through the application of localised heat and pressure. Two electrodes are positioned on two or more sheets of metal, and a defined force profile is applied. The electrical current generates resistive heating at the interface between the sheets, and a molten fusion zone is formed. At the end of this automated process, the electrodes are removed.

For cathodic protection [ 3 ], the sheets are electrogalvanised, but during subsequent welding operations, this thin surface layer liquefies at temperatures above 419 °C and potentially leads to liquid metal embrittlement (LME). In the worst case, LME can cause liquid metal-induced cracking (LMC) and ultimately result in total failure. Occurring surface cracks form and propagate intergranularly [ 4 ,  5 ]; i.e. the formerly ductile steel shows brittle cracking behaviour with significantly reduced plastic deformation [ 6 ,  7 ].

Regarding the susceptibility to the occurrence of LME at the sheet surface, the specific type of material pairing, the temperature range achieved during welding, the level of plastic deformation, and the rate of loading are the main factors [ 8 ,  9 ,  10 ,  11 – 12 ] and are directly linked to process parameters. The thermal loading is correlated with the welding time and welding current. Furthermore, the electrode force influences the electrical contact between the welded sheets, which, in turn, impacts the temperature. Additional influences arise from the electrode geometry and the shaft cooling, which affect the temperature and the stress distribution in the sheets. Insufficient cooling after welding causes reheating of the sheet surface and thus poses another major influence on LMC [ 13 ]. Other influences on LME include the welding calliper, the electrode type, and the electrode alloy. The method of galvanisation, the microstructure, and alloying elements also contribute to LME susceptibility [ 14 ,  15 ]. Additionally, the base material itself plays a significant role in embrittlement [ 16 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ].

It was found that hot tensile tests provide valuable insights into the onset and the growth of LME cracks [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]. LME susceptibility can be determined with various experimental approaches, such as tests with residual stresses in cups, welding experiments with different steel grades, or welding experiments under external loading conditions [ 24 ,  25 ,  26 – 27 ].

It was found that high electrode force, low current, and reduced welding time help to minimise LME [ 28 ]. However, reducing the welding time or current decreases heat input, which not only mitigates LME but also results in weaker weld spots [ 29 ]. Methods like pulsed current or ramped current have positive effects on LME while still achieving a satisfactory weld spot [ 30 ]. Optimising the holding time after welding is beneficial to prevent LME [ 13 ]. Using rounded electrode tip profiles instead of standard ones causes less embrittlement due to improved stress and temperature distribution in the sheets [ 31 ]. Furthermore, the influence of the electrode alloy must be considered [ 32 ]. Inserting thin aluminium sheets between the electrode and steel sheet was found to reduce LME, with the downside of adding additional complexity to the process [ 33 ].

This study seeks to identify and mitigate the risk of liquid metal embrittlement (LME) during resistance spot welding of DP1200HD, while simultaneously enhancing the weld spot quality. The influence of key process parameters is systematically analysed, including the electrode base material, electrode surface coating, electrode front face geometry, welding current magnitude, weld time, and post-weld hold time. The primary objective is to determine optimised parameter combinations that effectively reduce or eliminate intergranular cracking caused by LME.

This research introduces two key innovations. First, the use of refractory metal-based electrodes improves thermal and chemical stability at the electrode-sheet interface. Second, a novel electrode front face geometry improves contact conditions and tailors local thermal gradients. Both approaches are evaluated for their impact on the incidence, morphology, and propagation behaviour of LME cracks. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into LME mitigation strategies and contribute to advancing the understanding of electrode design and process optimisation for material systems prone to LME.

sections.heading: Methodology
paragraphs: This research presents a new approach to reduce LME based on newly developed electrode alloys in comparison to standard copper alloys. Different refractory materials, such as molybdenum and tungsten, are used during welding, and LME is significantly reduced. Furthermore, methods such as the recently patented [ 34 ] clothoidal electrodes and an adapted welding process are demonstrated in this work.

The applied combination of numerical modelling and extensive testing leads to the identification of beneficial parameter combinations and a reduction of LME. The subsequent sections provide an overview of the applied experimental and numerical methods.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: The investigated sheet material is an advanced high-strength dual-phase steel with a yield strength of 1200 MPa and high ductility (DP1200HD) featuring a fracture strain of 14% as measured on a Gleeble® 3800 thermomechanical simulator. The microstructure consists of bainitic-ferrite and martensite, with a composition of 0.2% (mass per cent) C, 1.5% Si, 2.5% Mn, and balanced Fe, determined using optical emission spectrometry. The DP1200HD sheets were electrogalvanised with a homogeneous pure zinc layer of 7-µm thickness. The interested reader can find further details on the material in [ 22 ].

This work focuses on sheet material with 1.6-mm thickness, while various stack-ups are manufactured by spot welding two or three identical sheets. The electrode caps are not re-machined during experiments to ensure comparable findings, while every welding configuration is replicated five times. The standard electrode shape is an F1-16–20-5.5 (here F1-electrode) with a front face diameter of 5.5 mm, as further specified in Deutsches Institut für Normung [ 35 ], and the direct welding current is determined by the methods described in SEP1220-2 [ 36 ]. The specified standard welding time is 380 ms, holding time equalled 300 ms, and the electrode force is 4.5 kN.

A C-calliper equipped with a Nimak pedestal welder and a Matuschek controller is used for placing weld spots with varying electrode materials and electrode surface coatings, as described below. Standard uncoated electrodes are machined from copper (CuCrZr) and serve as a benchmark, and are compared to other electrode materials. Uncoated molybdenum-copper (MoCu30) electrodes contain 70% molybdenum and 30% copper. WL10 electrodes are machined from tungsten and afterwards carbide-coated. TZM electrodes consist of titanium, zirconium, and molybdenum, and different coatings are investigated. Pure titanium nitride (TiN_175) is applied by physical vapour deposition (PVD). C235 and C230 coatings are deposited via chemical vapour deposition (CVD). C235 is made of TiN-TiB 2 , and C230 is a multi-layered TiCN-TiN/TiNB coating. The main material properties of CuCrZr [ 37 ,  38 ], TZM, and WL10, respectively, are shown in Table  1 . The material properties for MoCu30 are assumed to be identical to those of CuCrZr.

In the first experimental setup, three-sheet stack-ups are produced with the different electrode types to investigate possible influences on LME. In a second series, the focus is placed on variations of the electrode geometry and welding schedules using an X-calliper with uncoated CuCrZr electrodes. In this series, two-sheet stack-ups are welded. The surfaces of all weld spots are digitised and de-zincified with hydrochloric acid. Afterwards, dye penetration tests are conducted, and micrographs of Nital etched weld spots were investigated to visualise potential cracks. The micrographs are automatically evaluated with ImageJ [ 39 ]. Table  2  shows the welding parameters for the analysed weld spots. sections.heading: Finite element modelling
paragraphs: The validated multi-physical models [ 22 ] developed within the commercial finite element package Abaqus 2019 [ 40 ] simulate the entire welding process, including electrical, thermal, mechanical, and metallurgical quantities. Metallurgical effects, such as phase transformations including liquid and multiple solid phases, and a physically based LME damage indicator are implemented with FORTRAN-based user-defined subroutines. A detailed description of the multi-physical welding model can be found in Prabitz, Pichler, et al. [ 22 ], and the local damage indicator is described in Prabitz, Asadzadeh, et al. [ 23 ].

In the first step, representative single-element tests are used to verify the implementation of the material model and to show the predictive quality in comparison to thermo-mechanical experiments. Subsequently, the validated material model is integrated with a multi-physical 3D model of thermo-mechanical experiments, which enables the validation of the local damage indicator. It is important to note that, in addition to the temperature-dependent flow curves, the experiments provide information on the LME damage, which depends on the local temperature history, strain rate, and fracture strain.

Finally, a fully coupled 3D axisymmetric wedge resistance spot welding (RSW) model is employed to represent the welding process. The meshes of the electrodes and sheets consist of a structured mesh with Q3D8 hexahedral elements as well as wedge Q3D6 elements along the vertical axis of the model, with an approximate element size of 0.1 mm and a coarser swept mesh further away from the contact region [ 22 ]. For the sheet, a structured mesh with the same element types is applied, with an element size matching the electrode mesh in the contact region and progressively coarsening further away. All relevant electrical, thermal, and mechanical boundary conditions are shown in Fig.  1 . The RSW model with the local damage indicator is again validated against a large number of welding experiments. The models are described in detail in previous publications [ 6 ,  21 ,  22 – 23 ,  41 ]. Fig. 1 The meshed RSW model with an overview of the electrical, thermal, and mechanical boundary conditions

sections.heading: Results and discussion
paragraphs: The first part of the results section focuses on the knowledge obtained from numerical variations of electrode geometry and process parameters. The second part presents insight into the results from the two experimental test series.

sections.heading: Welding simulations
paragraphs: The RSW finite element model enables the prediction of configurations that reduce LME and improve weldability compared to the standard process. Figure  2 a illustrates the model for a weldspot with F1-electrodes at the region of interest (ROI) marked in magenta. It is important to note that this work develops a novel electrode cap geometry with an optimised clothoidal shape, which is denoted as K-electrode and depicted in Fig.  2 b. The front face of the electrode matches the F1-electrodes with a front face radius of 5.5 mm while showing no discontinuity. The detailed geometrical description is provided in Prabitz, Antretter, et al. [ 41 ] and Seibold and Prabitz [ 42 ]. In Fig.  2 c, the time-dependent strain rate is shown to be similar for the weld spot conducted with the F1-electrodes (orange) and with the K-electrodes (blue). The last peak of the strain rate at around  t  = 1.2 s does not result in additional damage because it occurs at low local temperatures. LME is observed for strain rates of 0.01 s −1  up to 0.1 s −1  and between 750 and 687.5 °C, respectively, for DP1200HD. The onset and evolution of LME are examined with hot tensile tests conducted with a Gleeble® 3800, as shown in Prabitz, Asadzadeh, et al. [ 23 ]. Note that the twofold welding time applied here leads to an overall higher thermal loading and an elevated electrode penetration compared to the standard welding time. Weld spots with the F1-electrode experience a longer period above the critical temperatures (see Fig.  2 e) and show higher strains due to electrode penetration (see Fig.  2 d). A higher degree of damage is expected, as indicated by the damage indicator in Fig.  2 f. Additional stresses may also arise due to electrode misalignment and sharp edges, which are mitigated using the K-electrodes. The specific welding conditions were  I  (welding current) = 6.9 kA,  F el  (electrode force) = 4.5 kN,  t weld  (welding time) = 760 ms, and  t hold  (holding time) = 300 ms. The typical F1-electrodes feature a distinct transition between the front face radius and the adjoining spherical transition region on the lateral electrode face. During welding, the front face of the electrode penetrates the sheet metal, generating tensile stresses on the surface of the sheet in the transition region. Additionally, elevated temperatures arise due to reduced air cooling in this area. These combined factors—mechanical stress and high temperature—serve as the primary macroscopic contributors to liquid metal embrittlement (LME), highlighting the importance of studying the region of interest (ROI). Fig. 2 ROI indicated in magenta for the weld spot with  a  F1-electrodes and  b  K-electrodes. Time-dependent  c  strain rate,  d  strain,  e  temperature, and  f  damage indicator for the ROI for the F1-electrode weld spot (orange) and the K-electrode weld spot (blue),  I  = 6.9 kA,  F el  = 4.5 kN,  t weld  = 760 ms,  t hold  = 300 ms

Internal electrode cooling and subsequent cooling of the sheets significantly affect the cracking tendency. Figure  3  illustrates the relevant quantities triggering LME for disrupted cooling by removing the F1-electrodes after the welding process. For the modified case (blue), no cooling is applied, while for the standard case (orange), cooling is applied for 300 ms. In the no-cooling scenario, the electrode caps are removed from the weld spot to eliminate cooling through contact. Vertical red lines indicate the start of the cooling cycle. As shown in Fig.  3 , the absence of cooling results in significant reheating after welding, especially in the area of the electrode indentation. This subsequently leads to a higher strain rate (Fig.  3 b) and higher strain (Fig.  3 c) depending on the thermal expansion. Consequently, a higher risk of damage at the ROI is predicted by the damage indicator, as seen in Fig.  3 e. The welding parameters are  I  = 6.2 kA,  F el  = 3.0 kN, and  t weld  = 380 ms. Fig. 3 a  ROI of the F1-electrode,  b  strain rate,  c  strain,  d  temperature, and  e  time-dependent damage indicator; blue lines indicate the process without cooling and orange the standard process, vertical red lines indicate the start of the holding period. Welding parameters:  I  = 6.2 kA,  F el  = 3.0 kN, and  t weld  = 380 ms.

Additional simulations with varying ramps of the welding current and the electrode force are conducted. An ascending current does not show any significant improvement. According to the model, descending currents reduce LME because surface temperatures of the base steel remain below the critical temperature. Similar findings are reported in Digiovanni et al. [ 43 ] and Ling et al. [ 44 ], where a decreasing welding current performs better given LME than standard welding processes.

Typically, copper electrodes are used in the automotive industry, and it remains an open question if the electrode material influences the embrittlement. It is assumed that different electrodes alter the electrical and thermal contact conditions, resulting in different thermal and mechanical loading of the sheet material. For the sake of simplicity, contact properties are taken from [ 22 ] and remain unchanged for each individual electrode material. RSW models accounting for each electrode material, i.e. CuCrZr, TZM, and WL10, are developed. The aim is to quantify the influence of the electrode material on LME.

Simulation results in Fig.  4  provide information about the temperature distribution at the end of the welding cycle for a three-sheet weld spot and three different F1-electrode materials. The relevant region is again marked in magenta. In Fig.  4 a, the temperature of the electrodes after welding with a CuCrZr electrode is lower than after welding with the TZM electrode depicted in (b) or with the WL10 electrode in (c). Due to lower thermal conductivity, the TZM and WL10 electrodes experience higher internal heating than the CuCrZr electrodes. Higher thermal loading of the TZM and WL10 electrodes results in higher wear of the electrodes and a higher LME risk. Despite the higher temperatures of the electrodes, the temperature distribution in the sheets is comparable. Thus, at this point, no clear statement of whether the electrode alloy influences LME can be given. For each configuration, the same welding parameters are applied:  I  = 6.2 kA,  F el  = 3.0 kN,  t weld  = 380 ms, and  t hold  = 300 ms. Fig. 4 Temperature distribution at the end of the welding process when welding with  a  CuCrZr,  b  TZM, and  c  WL10 F1-electrodes. Welding parameters:  I  = 6.2 kA,  F el  = 4.5 kN,  t weld  = 380 ms, and  t hold  = 300 ms

sections.heading: Influence of electrode material and coating type
paragraphs: The question remains whether the CuCrZr electrode alloy influences the LME occurrence as compared to other electrode materials. For different electrodes, the applicable welding current range varies significantly and is found to be reduced for the new MoCu30, WL10, and TZM electrodes. For information on the process of welding current determination, refer to Stahlinstitut VDEh [ 36 ]. Single and double welding times do not show any difference in LME, while the fivefold welding time presented here produces robust outcomes for three-sheet stack-ups welded with different electrodes: MoCu30 alloy electrodes result in significant embrittlement comparable to the standard CuCrZr caps (see Fig.  5 a). High wear of the MoCu30 electrodes at the electrode face, as well as a reduced welding current range, was found. Furthermore, at the electrode surface, intermetallic phases formed from copper and zinc. The WL10 electrodes with carbide coating fail during mounting due to brittle shattering or coolant leakage, rendering them unsuitable for testing. TZM electrodes with TiN_175 coating exhibit significantly reduced LMC (see Fig.  5 b). However, the TiN_175 coating develops cracks at the contact face, and zinc accumulates beside the electrode shoulder. Although the C235 coating of the TZM electrodes has disappeared completely at the contact area, it is found to be intact on the sides. The C235 coating exhibits low wear resistance. Despite the absence of a coating layer, LME is notably reduced with this electrode type, as visible in Fig.  5 c. This suggests that the TZM base material of the electrodes has a significant influence on LME. The TZM electrode caps with the C230 coating reduce LME. The corresponding micrograph of a sample with the fivefold welding time is shown in Fig.  5 d, revealing some minor cracks. The C230 coating remained intact, and no significant zinc pick-up is observed. Fig. 5 a  MoCu30 (weld spot 10) electrodes lead to massive embrittlement comparable to standard caps, while  b  TZM-TiN_175 (weld spot 11),  c  TZM-C235 (weld spot 12), and  d  TZM-C230 (weld spot 13) led to hardly any embrittlement, although fivefold welding time was applied.

Electrode coatings offer anti-adhesion and thermal-barrier effects that inhibit zinc wetting and stabilise the electrode–sheet contact. Maintaining adequate electrode force ensures even pressure distribution, improves contact resistance control, accelerates cooling, and limits zinc penetration—all reducing LME crack length. High electrode electrical conductivity decreases self-heating, enhancing temperature control, while high hardness prevents local plastic deformation and further LME initiation.

While Fig.  5 a shows massive LME cracks with lengths up to 1800 µm after welding with MoCu30 electrodes, the welds with other electrodes, as displayed in Fig.  5 b to d, do not exhibit significant LME cracks deeper than 30 µm. This may indicate that copper or brass alloys somehow promote LME, which agrees with the findings of Savage et al. [ 45 ].

It is also evident that alternative electrode materials result in a temperature distribution that differs from standard electrodes, which, in turn, leads to a different deformation behaviour of the welds. Higher electrical contact resistance between the sheet and TZM electrodes causes increased heating at the surface and is identified as a reason for excessive surface deformation and reduced weldability. The higher probability of contraction cavities may be mitigated by an adapted welding current.

Figure  5 a to d show the different zones in the weld spot, such as the base material, the heat-affected zone (HAZ), and the fusion zone (FZ). The base material consists of approximately 50% ferrite, 40% martensite, and 10% retained austenite. After welding, the FZ in the centre solidifies in columnar, elongated grains. High cooling rates in this region lead to a mainly martensitic microstructure. In the HAZ, grain coarsening occurs near the fusion boundary, while the microstructure mainly depends on the cooling rates. Noticeable LMC occurs in the HAZ penetrating the sheets perpendicularly, while some minor cracks can be found beneath the electrode cap in the electrode intend where the material is cooled through conductivity.

sections.heading: Further methods to reduce LME
paragraphs: In literature [ 46 ], rounded electrode tips are found to reduce LME; however, some of these shapes are not practical in real-world processes. Therefore, the K-electrode tip shape is developed in this work to provide good weldability and a reduction of embrittlement, as already indicated by the numerical models [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ,  34 ]. The K-electrodes offer improved compensation of calliper misalignment, whereas welding with the standard F1-electrodes shows that even a small misalignment can result in significant embrittlement.

Weld spot 1, produced with F1-electrodes and an electrode force of 3.0 kN, exhibits large cracks, whereas the comparable weld spot 6, created with K-electrodes, shows only minor cracks (see Fig.  6 ). A similar conclusion is drawn for 4.5 kN at weld spot 4 (F1-electrode) and weld spot 9 (K-electrode), demonstrating that the use of K-electrodes leads to reduced embrittlement. These new electrodes prove to be particularly beneficial for low electrode forces and elongated welding times. Lower electrode forces result in reduced contact between the sheets, which subsequently leads to higher contact resistances. This, in turn, causes higher temperatures at the interfaces and a higher risk of LME. The reduction of LME with elevated electrode forces is also reported in Choi et al. [ 47 ]. Higher forces cause larger deformations at the sheet surface, which is undesirable due to the high-quality requirements of the surface. Fig. 6 Maximum crack depth and the maximum circumferential crack lengths for each specimen as defined in Table  3

Ascending and descending currents are applied separately. A current starting at 90% of the maximum current and finishing at 110% results in the massive expulsion of molten steel. Conversely, a current starting at 110% and ending at 90% does not show significant improvements regarding LME. However, a current starting at 110% and ending at 70%, as applied for weld spot 5, proves to be beneficial compared to the standard process seen in weld spot 4. This finding is consistent with the results reported by DiGiovanni et al. [ 43 ]. The reduction of LME can be explained by the temperature evolution, which declines beneath the critical threshold during the adaptation process; hence, the conditions for initiating LME are no longer present. Adapting the current schedule is a comparatively cost-effective means of inhibiting LME. Table  3  summarises the welding conditions applied, as shown in Fig.  6 .

According to model results and experimental investigations from this study, as well as findings in the literature [ 13 ], a specific holding time after welding is essential to minimise embrittlement beneath the electrode indentation. Böhne et al. demonstrate that a certain holding time is mandatory for optimal results, but there is potential for a case-dependent optimisation of its duration. In this work, the standard holding time of 300 ms is compared to the case without any holding time. With holding and using F1-electrodes, no significant LME is observed for weld spot 3, whereas weld spot 2 without holding exhibits some embrittlement. For welds with K-electrodes and typical holding times, weld spot 8 shows minor LME, whereas the absence of holding results in large cracks in weld spot 7. The behaviour is attributed to the reheating effect of the sheet’s surface, which increases the cracking tendency as predicted by the numerical models. The cracks detected in the experiments for the holding time are more pronounced when using K caps.

The maximum depths of LME cracks, determined from micrographs, and the maximum lengths measured using surface dye penetration tests, are shown in Fig.  6 . A lower risk of LME is observed for the configurations welded with K-electrodes as well as for those using special electrode alloys.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: Spot welding is assessed numerically using validated finite element models. Based on these models, an optimised welding schedule is derived, which leads to a significant reduction of liquid metal embrittlement. The electrode material is found to have the most noticeable impact on embrittlement. Without changing the electrode material, the electrode shape leads to a significant reduction of LME, while the process design has a subordinate impact. The following conclusions can be drawn: Surface-coated electrodes from refractory material are an effective measure to reduce and avoid embrittlement. This suggests that the standard copper electrodes affect the susceptibility of the base steel to embrittlement. The electrode alloy, surface coating, and welding conditions should be fine-tuned in further studies. Newly developed K-electrodes result in a significant reduction of critical stresses around the weld spot, as well as a reduction of stresses caused by misalignment of the standard electrodes. Both effects contribute to a significant reduction of embrittlement while also providing improved weldability. A mandatory holding time after welding significantly reduces liquid metal embrittlement in the sheets beneath the electrode indentation. Interrupted cooling induces reheating, which leads to critical conditions for embrittlement. This finding is observed to be independent of the electrode shape. A downwards ramped current has a beneficial effect on the surface conditions of the sheets to the extent that the weld spot may become insensitive to embrittlement.
